key_terms.meaning: Three-terminal resistor with a sliding wiper; for wiper at distance x on a track of length L, output V₀ = (x/L)·V_s where V_s is the supply voltage.
Output volts per unit displacement, S = V_s/L (V/m) for a linear track, or V_s/θ_max for a rotary one.
Fall in output voltage when the measuring circuit draws current; it is nearly zero if the load resistance is far larger than the potentiometer resistance.
Smallest displacement the wiper can distinguish; a wire-wound track with N turns gives resolution ≈ L/N.
A thin metal foil or wire grid bonded to a surface; when the surface stretches or compresses, the grid resistance changes.
GF = (ΔR/R)/(ΔL/L) = (ΔR/R)/ε; about 2 for metal foil gauges, 50 to 200 for semiconductor gauges.
Strain at right angles to the gauge axis also changes resistance; the folded grid shape of a foil gauge cancels most of this error.
Doped silicon bar whose resistance changes strongly with strain through the piezoresistive effect; high GF but strong temperature dependence.
Four-resistor bridge that converts ΔR/R into a voltage; a single active arm gives V₀ ≈ (V_s/4)·(ΔR/R) at small strain.
A machined elastic element (column, beam or ring) carrying four bonded gauges in a bridge; output is calibrated in newtons or kilograms.
Gauges fixed at ±45° to the shaft axis measure shear strain; shear stress τ = T·r/J, so torque T follows from the bridge output.
Resistance temperature detector: a pure platinum or nickel winding whose resistance rises almost linearly with temperature.
R(T) = R₀[1 + αT + βT² + …], the polynomial that fits an RTD resistance over its full range.
Sintered metal-oxide ceramic with a large negative temperature coefficient; R = R₀·exp[B(1/T − 1/T₀)], with B in kelvin.
A fine heated wire placed in a flow; King's law h = A + B·v^0.5 links the cooling to velocity v, and the wire resistance reveals the cooling.
A moisture-absorbing film whose resistance falls as water vapour is adsorbed; it is calibrated directly in relative humidity (%RH).
Cadmium sulphide or similar semiconductor whose resistance drops as light intensity E rises, roughly R ≈ A·E^(−γ).
A material such as indium antimonide, or a thin magnetic multilayer, whose resistance rises in a magnetic field; used for contactless position and speed sensing.
Two dissimilar metals joined at two points produce an emf E = α(T_hot − T_cold), where α is the Seebeck coefficient in µV/°C.
Circuit or software that measures the reference junction temperature and adds it back, so the displayed value is the hot-junction temperature.

takeaways: A potentiometer is the simplest displacement sensor: displacement sets the wiper position, the divider sets the voltage, and the only serious error is loading by the measuring circuit.
A strain gauge turns mechanical strain into a fractional resistance change, and the gauge factor is the single constant that links the two.
Metal foil gauges are linear and stable; semiconductor gauges are far more sensitive but need temperature compensation.
The Wheatstone bridge is the standard signal-conditioning circuit for every resistive sensor in this unit, because it reads small ΔR/R without being swamped by the large standing resistance.
Shape the elastic element properly and a strain gauge measures force, weight or torque with a calibration that is fixed by geometry, not by the electronics.
RTDs are accurate and near-linear but slow; thermistors are very sensitive but nonlinear and limited in range; choosing between them is a trade of linearity against sensitivity.
The same resistance–temperature relation that makes a hot wire cool also makes it a flow sensor, which is why hot-wire anemometry is a temperature measurement in disguise.
Photon and magnetic-field sensors are passive resistors with no moving parts, which makes them cheap, rugged and easy to interface to a bridge.
A thermocouple needs no excitation and works to very high temperatures, but its accuracy depends entirely on knowing or compensating the cold junction.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a labelled construction sketch, the governing formula with each symbol defined, a short derivation, a worked numerical example and a list of practical errors with their remedies.

bank.q: Define gauge factor. Derive its expression for a single metal wire strain gauge using the resistance formula R = ρL/A, and explain why the value for a metal gauge is close to 2.
outline: R = ρL/A written with each symbol defined
Logarithmic differentiation giving ΔR/R = Δρ/ρ + ΔL/L − ΔA/A
Area change from Poisson's ratio: ΔA/A = −2ν·ε
Result GF = 1 + 2ν + (Δρ/ρ)/ε
For metals the resistivity term is small and ν ≈ 0.3, so GF ≈ 2
Comment: semiconductor gauges get their large GF from the resistivity term

bank.q: Describe the construction of a wire-wound and a conductive-film potentiometer used as a displacement sensor. Explain, with a circuit diagram, how the output voltage becomes proportional to displacement and what limits its accuracy.
outline: Former, mandrel, resistance wire or film, wiper, end connections
Circuit as a voltage divider: V₀ = (x/L)·V_s
Sensitivity S = V_s/L in V/m
Resolution set by number of turns, L/N
Loading error when the meter resistance is not much larger than the track resistance
Friction, wear, backlash and nonlinearity of the winding

bank.q: State and explain the three laws of thermoelectric circuits. Show how the law of intermediate metals allows copper leads to be used in a thermocouple circuit.
outline: Law of homogeneous material: a temperature gradient along one wire alone produces no emf
Law of intermediate metals: an inserted third metal at the same temperature changes nothing
Law of intermediate temperatures: E(T₁,T₃) = E(T₁,T₂) + E(T₂,T₃)
Application of the second law to copper connecting leads and terminal blocks
Practical consequence: only the two junction temperatures matter

bank.q: Compare a platinum RTD, a thermistor and a thermocouple for temperature measurement in the range 0–400 °C under the headings: sensing principle, sensitivity, linearity, range, excitation, speed of response and cost.
outline: RTD: metal resistance rise, near linear, needs excitation current, wide range, moderate cost
Thermistor: ceramic, large negative coefficient, nonlinear, narrow range, needs excitation, fast, cheap
Thermocouple: Seebeck emf, no excitation, very wide range, needs cold-junction compensation
Sensitivity figures: about 0.385 Ω/Ω per °C for Pt, several percent per °C for a thermistor, about 40 µV/°C for a type-K pair
Self-heating in RTD and thermistor but not in thermocouple
Conclusion: match the sensor to range, accuracy and speed needs

bank.q: A linear potentiometer has a 100 mm track, a supply of 10 V and a wire winding of 500 turns. Find the sensitivity in V/mm, the output for a wiper at 35 mm, and the resolution in millimetres. The wiper feeds a voltmeter of 1 MΩ and the track resistance is 5 kΩ. Estimate the loading error at mid-travel.
outline: Resolution = L/N = 100/500 = 0.2 mm
Divider output at mid-travel is 5 V, Thevenin resistance about 1.25 kΩ
Error fraction ≈ R_th/R_meter ≈ 0.125 %, about 6 mV
Conclusion: loading error is negligible with a high-impedance meter

bank.q: A 120 Ω foil strain gauge with gauge factor 2.1 forms one arm of a Wheatstone bridge excited at 4 V. The surface strain is 600 microstrain. Find the resistance change, the open-circuit bridge output, and the output if all four arms are active with two in tension and two in compression.
outline: Quarter-bridge output V₀ = (V_s/4)·GF·ε = 1.26 mV
Full-bridge with opposite arms gives four times this: 5.04 mV
Note the output is small, so an instrumentation amplifier of gain 100–1000 follows
Mention that the full-bridge also cancels axial temperature effects

bank.q: A Pt100 RTD has R₀ = 100 Ω at 0 °C and α = 0.00385 /°C. Using the Callendar–Van Dusen equation with β = 0 (below 0 °C correction ignored), find its resistance at 80 °C and the change in resistance per °C at that temperature. Suggest a bridge arrangement to read it.
outline: Compare with a 10 kΩ thermistor giving hundreds of ohms per °C
Three-wire bridge or a constant-current source with a differential amplifier
Lead resistance must be cancelled; keep excitation current small to limit self-heating

bank.q: A thermistor with B = 3900 K and R = 10 kΩ at 25 °C is used to measure 60 °C. Calculate its resistance, the resistance change per °C near 60 °C, and comment on the linearisation needed.
outline: R = R₀·exp[B(1/T − 1/T₀)] with T in kelvin (333 K and 298 K)
Exponent B × that = −1.376, so R ≈ 10 kΩ × 0.2525 ≈ 2.5 kΩ
Sensitivity near 60 °C from dR/dT = −(B/T²)·R, roughly −0.11 kΩ/°C
Nonlinearity handled by a series/shunt pad, a lookup table or a log amplifier
Compare: an RTD at the same point changes by fractions of an ohm per °C

bank.q: A hot-wire anemometer follows King's law V² = A + B·v^0.5, where V is the voltage across the wire and v the air speed. Two calibration points give V = 4.0 V at v = 0 and V = 6.0 V at v = 4 m/s. Predict the voltage at 9 m/s and explain how the bridge holds the wire temperature constant.
outline: A = 16 from the zero-flow point
At v = 4, v^0.5 = 2, so 36 = 16 + 2B giving B = 10
Constant-temperature mode: the wire is one arm of a feedback bridge held at fixed resistance
Higher flow cools the wire, resistance falls, feedback raises current to restore it
Output voltage is then a direct measure of cooling and hence of velocity
Note the square-root law and the need for temperature compensation of the air

bank.q: Analyse the sources of error in a bonded strain-gauge installation and evaluate the correction used for each: lead-wire resistance, temperature change of the gauge and the test piece, creep, and moisture.
outline: Lead resistance adds to the arm and reduces sensitivity: use three-wire or full-bridge connection
Apparent strain from differential expansion: use a dummy gauge or a self-temperature-compensated gauge
Resistivity and modulus both change with temperature: bridge has to cancel both
Creep and hysteresis from the adhesive and the carrier: choose correct adhesive and cure cycle
Moisture changes insulation resistance: use encapsulated gauges
Nonlinearity of semiconductor gauges and their strong temperature coefficient

bank.q: A load cell is to weigh bags of cement up to 50 kg. Design the measurement chain: elastic element shape, gauge placement, bridge configuration, excitation, amplification and calibration. Justify each choice.
outline: Column or double-bending beam chosen for the load magnitude and for compactness
Four gauges, two in tension and two in compression, forming a full bridge
Full bridge gives four times the quarter-bridge output and cancels axial and temperature effects
Excitation chosen so that self-heating in the gauges stays low, typically a few volts
Instrumentation amplifier with high common-mode rejection, then a low-pass filter
Calibration with dead weights and a check of zero, span, creep and return-to-zero
Mention overload stops and the protection against eccentric loading

bank.q: Compare a thermocouple, an RTD and a thermistor for measuring a patient's body temperature in the range 35–42 °C in a hospital setting. Evaluate sensitivity, linearity, safety, size and cost, and state your recommendation.
outline: Range is narrow, so the sensor must resolve 0.1 °C or better
Thermistor: fast, small, high sensitivity, cheap; needs linearisation and has drift
RTD: stable and repeatable, good for calibration reference, but larger and slower
Thermocouple: robust and tiny but needs a cold junction and its sensitivity is low near body temperature
Excitation and self-heating must be limited to keep the probe from warming the tissue
Recommendation: thermistor in a disposable probe for routine use, RTD for a reference thermometer

bank.q: Evaluate four methods of cold-junction compensation for a thermocouple measuring a furnace at about 900 °C: ice bath, isothermal block with a semiconductor sensor, bridge circuit with a temperature-sensitive resistor, and software compensation with a stored table.
outline: Ice bath: most accurate reference but impractical for plant use
Isothermal block with a thermistor or IC sensor: standard practice, good to about 0.5 °C
Compensating bridge in the instrument: simple but drifts and is hard to make accurate
Software with an ITS-90 table and a measured cold-junction value: flexible and now the norm
Also consider extension leads and their own thermoelectric voltages, and the law of intermediate metals
Conclusion: cold-junction error of 1 °C is a real error of about 1 °C at the hot junction because the emf is linear in the difference

glossary.def: Change in length divided by original length of a body, a dimensionless number usually quoted in microstrain (10⁻⁶).
Ratio of sideways contraction to lengthwise extension of a stretched material, about 0.3 for steel and aluminium.
Change of a material's resistivity caused by mechanical stress, the effect that gives semiconductor gauges their large gauge factor.
Active length of the resistance grid along the measuring axis; strain is averaged over this length.
The DC or AC supply voltage or current fed to a Wheatstone bridge, which sets the size of the output signal.
Bridge arrangements with one, two or four active gauge arms, giving output in the ratio 1 : 2 : 4.
An unstrained gauge mounted on the same material and placed in the adjacent bridge arm to cancel temperature effects.
Rise in a sensor's own temperature caused by the measuring current, an error source in RTDs and thermistors.
Fractional change of resistance per degree Celsius, 0.00385 /°C for platinum and negative and large for an NTC thermistor.
RTD wiring in which the lead resistances cancel in the bridge, leaving only the sensor resistance.
Slow change of sensor output under a steady load, caused by the adhesive or the elastic element settling.
Difference between the readings taken while loading and while unloading, for the same applied quantity.
Change in output divided by the change in input that caused it, with units such as V/mm or Ω/°C.
Difference between the upper and lower limits of the measurable range of a sensor.
The sliding contact of a potentiometer that taps a fraction of the track and carries the output voltage.
Water vapour actually present in air as a percentage of the maximum the air can hold at that temperature.
Emf produced per degree of junction temperature difference, quoted in µV/°C and specific to each metal pair.
The thermocouple junction held at a known temperature, whose value must be added to the measured emf.
Several thermocouples in series to multiply the emf, used in radiation sensors and gas detectors.
Any circuit or software step that converts a curved sensor characteristic into a straight line over the working range.
Maximum deviation of the sensor output from the best straight line, expressed as a percentage of full-scale output.
Negative temperature coefficient thermistor, whose resistance falls as temperature rises.
Instrument for measuring fluid flow speed; the hot-wire form uses the cooling of a heated resistor.
Light-dependent resistor, another name for a photoresistor used in light-operated switches and exposure meters.
